text: You start with a tree on n nodes, then one extra edge is added, giving a graph with n nodes and n edges. Return an edge that can be removed so the result is a tree again. If several answers exist, return the one that appears last in the input.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — since it was a tree plus one edge, the graph has exactly one cycle, and the removable edge is any edge on that cycle. Is that right?
Exactly. And when multiple cycle edges qualify, return the last one in the list.
Are the nodes labeled one to n? That affects the array size.

Let me run through an example. Edges one-two, one-three, two-three. The first two edges build a little tree over one, two and three. The third edge, two-three, connects two nodes that are already joined, closing the triangle — so the answer is two, three.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach is, for each edge, to run a DFS and see if its endpoints are already connected — that's n squared. This problem reminds me of cycle detection with Union-Find, because an edge closes a cycle exactly when its two endpoints are already in the same set. So I process edges in order and merge endpoints, and the first edge whose endpoints are already together is the one that closes the cycle — I return it. Because I scan in input order, that first failing edge is automatically the last cycle edge in the list, which is exactly the tie-break the problem wants. It's n times inverse Ackermann, effectively linear.

Here's the plan. One: a parent array where a negative value marks a root and its size, sized n plus one for one-indexing. Two: walk the edges in order and union each one. Three: the first time Union fails, return that edge. One thing worth flagging — Union returns false exactly when Find of u equals Find of v, meaning this edge would create a cycle. And a sizing detail — nodes go up to n, so the parent array must have length n plus one, not n, or I'd index out of bounds. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Find uses path compression, and Union merges by size and returns a bool: false when both roots are the same. The number of nodes equals the number of edges, so I size parent to n plus one. Then I walk the edges and return the first one whose Union fails. One thing worth flagging — one Union per edge is enough, and I check its result right there. A second, unchecked call on the same edge would be harmless — both ends already share a root, so it just returns false and changes nothing — but it's dead code.

Let's dry-run the code on one-two, one-three, two-three, expected two, three. The first two edges each merge two different roots, so node one becomes the root of all three. The row that matters is edge two-three: both Finds return one, so Union returns false, and I return two, three. A larger case: one-two, two-three, three-four, one-four, one-five. The first three build the chain one, two, three, four; then one-four finds its ends already connected, so it returns one, four — and one-five is never even reached. Correct.

Time is n times inverse Ackermann of n, effectively linear — one near-constant Union per edge. Space is linear for the parent array; I never build the graph. Oh, one more thing — the directed version of this problem is trickier: the extra edge can create a node with two parents, a directed cycle, or both, so you first find the two candidate edges into a node with in-degree two and reason about which to drop. Same Union-Find core, more casework.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You reduced removable edge to the first edge whose endpoints are already connected. You explained why input-order scanning gives the last-in-list tie-break for free. And you caught the n plus one sizing for one-indexed nodes. Good work.
